caseno: Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 36 of 1977
lawyer:
M. H. Khandker, Senior Advocate-----------For the Petitioner. 
Mian Abdul Gafur, Advocate, insructed by B.C. Pandey, Advocate-on-Record. Md. A. Aziz, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondents.

full_judgment:
2. Respondents secured a decree on 19-4-67 in a suit for ejectment from the premises in suit against the petitioner as a monthly tenant in respect of the said premises and the decree was affirmed by the appellate court on 24.2.68. Respondents, thereafter, put the decree in execution on 20-5-68 in O.C. Execution Case No. 190 of 1968 which was, however stayed during the pendancy of the Second Appeal which was preferred by the petitioner to the Dacca High Court against the appellate decree mentioned above. The Second Appeal was dismissed by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh on 8-1-74. When after the disposal of the Second Appeal, the proceeding of the execution case was resumed, an objection was filed by the petitioner on 12-3-74 in the said execution case under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. II of 1974. The objection taken therein was that the structures in respect of which the tenancy was created having been destroyed by fire during the pendency of the suit, the suit premises had become non-existent and as such the decree had became in executable. 

 5. Mr. K. H. Khandker, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the judgment-debtor petitioner, has strenuously argued that on the destruction by fire of the huts in respect of which the tenancy had been created the decree has become non-executable inasmuch as the subject matter, for the possession of which the decree was obtained, has become non-est. The tenancy was in respect of the huts only, learned Counsel submitted, and had nothing to do with the land on which the said huts stood and so there was nothing left to be taken possession of on the disappearance of the said huts, although the judgment-debtor was very much on the same site by constructing some new huts thereon. The argument seems to be of no substance on the very face of it. But Mr. Khondker with great persistence tried to add some amount of plausibility to such a patently wrong proposition by reference to some case law and the English principle relating to a statutory tenant. 

 6. The basic contention of the learned Counsel that the petitioner's tenancy consisted merely of the huts independently of the land on which the said huts stood appears to be based on some misconception. As a theoretical proposition it may not be an impossibility to have a tenancy of a hut or a room completely independent of the land on which the structure stands and it may be said, in case of a decree against the tenant in respect of such a hut or room, that the decree may become inexecutable on the destruction of such a hut or room, because with the disappearance of the hut or room in respect of which possession has been directed by the decree to be delivered, there remains nothing left to be complied with under the terms of the decree, as the possession of the tenant automatically comes to an end with the disappearance of the tenanted but or room in such a case. A tenancy of a room or apartment in a multi-storeyed building, which is incapable of being used or possessed by the tenant in any manner after its destruction, may be one of that sort of tenancy, but that is not the position in the instant case. 

 7. Learned Counsel has placed before us the description of the subject matter of the tenancy as given in the schedule to the plaint of the suit as well as of the decree passed therein, which has been quoted in paragraph 1 of the petition for leave. On a perusal of this description it becomes clear that the suit as well as the decree passed therein were in respect of the land within specified boundaries together with certain structures. In the local investigation which was held for the identity of the decretal premises the Advocate-Commissioner delineated the decretal premises with reference to the survey plots and it is the finding of the Courts below that the decretal land has been correctly described in the petition for execution. We have also examined the description of the premises as quoted in the petition for special leave and we find that it comprised a part of R. S. Plot No. 4953, appertaining to Khatian No. 3695 of Mouza Bakalia, known as Chaletai, with three huts standing thereon, which is the same as the new Municipal holding No. 264, and also the new Municipal holding No. 1863, surrounded on the north by the premises of another, Bharatia, Syed A. Majid. Sowdagar, on the south by that of the other bharatia, Rahman Brothers, on the east by Rajakhali Khal and on the west by the road. It is obvious that the subject matter of the tenancy comprised both lands and huts and as such on the destruction of the huts the entire subject Matter if the tenancy was not destroyed nor did the possession of the tenant in respect of the decretal premises automatically come to an end with such destruction. 

 8. Learned Counsel has cited a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman Sowdagar Vs. Sm. Emartannissa Begum, in (1970) 22 DLR 126 P.L.D 1957 Dacca 372: where a decree for recovery of possession on a declaration of title was affirmed by the High Court on the view that the monthly tenancy in question having been in respect of a but only was extinguished as such as the subject matter of the tenancy was completely gutted by fire and that the tenant who constructed a new but at the old site was not entitled to claim that his tenancy still subsisted at his option as contemplated in Section 108(e) of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 9. Mr. Khondker has also referred to a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of A. Motalib Vs. Mst. Rezia Begum, 22 D.L.R. (SC) 134 where the decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman was distinguished on the ground that the tenancy in that case was exclusively of a hut and so the subject matter of the lease could be said to have been destroyed as a whole and it was held that when a tenancy was in respect of some structures as well as of land the tenancy subsisted at the option of the tenant under section 108 (c) of the Transfer of Property Act, although all the structures were destroyed. 

 10. Learned Counsel has contended that it is the decision of the Dacca High Court, rather than the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court referred to above, which is applicable to the facts of the case and that the subject /matter of the tenancy, in view of the said decision, must be deemed to have come to an end on the destruction of the structures, as there has been nothing left in respect of which the decree may be executed. 

 11. We have already noticed that the tenancy in question was in respect of the land together with certain structures and as such if any of the aforesaid two" decisions is sought to be applicable to the instant case it is the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court which may be regarded to have some relevance. We are, however, not concerned in this case as to the conditions under which a tenancy may 'be extinguished, but we are to see here whether a decree, which has been obtained for recovery of possession of a Premises on the finding that the tenancy in question had already been extinguished has become inexecutable on the destruction of the structures which stood on the said premises. Such a decree may be inexecutable if the subject matter for the possession of which the decree has been made is completely destroyed, as in that event nothing may be left which may be taken possession of in executing the decree. In the instant case the tenant was in occupation of the land and structures as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint and the part of the land which was in possession of the tenant was covered by the structures and the remaining part was vacant. On the destruction of the huts the tenant continued to remain in possession of the land including the portion on which structures stood. In such a case, it is extremely difficult for the Court to accept the submission of the learned Counsel that on the destruction of the huts there was nothing left for the judgment-debtor to comply with and that the decree 'has become infructuous. It is not necessary for the disposal of this petition to decide Whether in view of the definition of "premises' as given in section 2(6) of East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, .1953, which means any building or part of the building or any hut or part of the but let, including the grounds appertaining to such building or 'hut or part thereof, there can be a tenancy of huts or structures independent of the land on which such structures stand, as has been held by the Dacca High Court in the case of Golamar Rahman Sowdagar and others, because, as we have already found in the instant case, the tenancy in question specifically comprised both land and structures. 

 12. Mr. Khandken, learned Counsel for the petitioner, has also referred to Halsbury's Laws of England Vol. 32, 3rd Edition paragraph 1586 page 806, where the position of what has been known in England a Statutory tenant has been explained. During the war time there had been in England certain legislations which are collectively known as Rent Restrictions Acts, for giving protection to or mitigating the hardships of certain categories of tenants, whose premises had been destroyed or damaged in consequence of the war. Under the English law, as has been stated in the said paragraph, a tenant who retains possession of the premises by virtue of the Rent Restrictions Act, is known as a Statutory tenant and his position is to be distinguished from that of a contractual tenant. Such a tenant is entitled to retain possession of the premises even after their contractual tenancy has been lawfully determined by notice to quit or otherwise and they are liable to be ejected only if the conditions laid down in the Rent Restrictions Acts are satisfied. Mr. Khandker has also cited two decisions of the English Court, namely, Ellis & Son Ltd. Vs. Sidman 1948(1) All. E.R. 461 and Eastend Dwellings Co. Ltd. Vs. Finsbury Borough Council 1951 (2) All, ER. 587., which dealt with the cases of a Statutory tenant whose rented premises were destroyed by enemy action. 'These cases which were decided on the basis of certain specific legislative enactments as are in force in England have no manner of application to the instant case. A lawful decree of the Court directing the judgment-debtor to remove himself from and vacate possession of the premises of which he is still admittedly in possession cannot be said to have been rendered inexecutable only because certain structures have been destroy act or demolished and certain new structures have been put up thereon. This Court pointed out the correct position of law in its order dated 19th December, 1975 rejecting Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 141 of 1975. The Courts below were right in rejecting the petitioner's plea. There is no substance in this petition which is dismissed.
